title: Models of Social Influence: Towards the Next Frontiers
publisher: Journal of Artificial Societies and Social Simulation 20(4) 2

key_points.claim: Review of the opinion dynamics/social influence modelling literature (Axelrod's question). It classifies models into three classes and names two frontiers: comparing and integrating models, and more empirical work.
key_points.evidence_quote: there is urgent need for more theoretical work comparing, relating and integrating alternative models. Second, the field suffers from a strong imbalance between a proliferation of theoretical studies and a dearth of empirical work.

key_points.claim: Bounded-confidence models (similarity bias, continuous opinions): a small confidence threshold fragments the population into opinion clusters; otherwise consensus results. Defuant and Hegselmann-Krause versions differ in updating, but core implications are the same.
key_points.evidence_quote: if the confidence level ε is sufficiently small, the population ends up fragmented in separate opinion clusters, while otherwise convergence towards consensus occurs

key_points.claim: Cultural-trait models (Axelrod 1997, nominal opinion vectors) combine homophily with influence on a lattice. Interaction stops when neighbours share nothing, so cultural diversity persists.
key_points.evidence_quote: interaction and thus influence becomes impossible if two neighbors have nothing in common.

key_points.claim: Homophily as a micro-assumption has structural and cognitive/emotional sources, which are formalised similarly but differ conceptually.
key_points.evidence_quote: Homophily may be caused by structural patterns of social interaction that systematically sort similar people into similar “foci”

key_points.claim: Repulsive influence models add differentiation, so weights turn negative for large disagreement. They generate bi-polarization and opinions more extreme than any initial opinion. Motivations: balance theory, cognitive dissonance, xenophobia, ego-involvement, and ingroup/outgroup identity.
key_points.evidence_quote: soon two clusters start to form at the opposite extremes of the spectrum, until eventually all agents have joined one of the two emergent factions.

key_points.claim: Empirical frontier: model assumptions are hard to test. Micro-level assumptions rest on 1950s-60s social-psychology experiments, so calibration and validation with experiments and data are needed.
key_points.evidence_quote: the assumptions of social-influence models, the dynamics that they generate, and also many of their predictions are notoriously difficult to put to the test.

key_points.claim: Examples of empirically calibrated ABMs of social influence: Afghan civil war opinions, political opinion distributions, agri-environmental policy diffusion among farmers, and climate-treaty negotiations.
key_points.evidence_quote: models extending the approaches discussed here have been calibrated and validated to study dynamics of citizens’ opinions about the conflicting forces in the Afghan civil war

key_points.claim: Social media and personalization algorithms are an emerging application. ABMs suggest personalization may contribute to polarization, but modelers have only just begun to address it.
key_points.evidence_quote: some warn that the personalization of Internet services can contribute to processes of opinion polarization (Dandekar et al. 2013; Mäs & Bischofberger 2015)

reliability_notes: Full text was read (PDF, peer-reviewed JASSS review, 2017). It covers only the opinion dynamics/social influence aspect of artificial societies, not the whole field. It is a few years old for a state-of-the-art summary. Quotes were taken from the extracted PDF text.
